payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Breakfast Is at Seven
by Corinne Abelard
The following passage is from a novel by Corinne Abelard. The narrator runs a boarding house in a small town on Lake Erie in the early 1950s.

```passage
    I have kept the house on Tolley Street for nineteen
years, and I can tell what has gone wrong with a person
by the way he comes down to breakfast. That November the
radiator in the dining room knocked all through the meal
like a relative who has been told twice that there is no
room. I served at seven. I have always served at seven.

    Mr. Halloran came first, as he always did, in the
brown suit he wore to sell fire and casualty to people
who did not believe in either. He had been promised the
district office in Lorain, and on Monday the district
office had gone to a man named Fisk who had been with
the company four years. Mr. Halloran did not tell me
this. He told me the lake was going to freeze early. He
buttered his toast to the very edges, the way a man
paints a fence he has been told is not his, and he said
"Early, mark me" three times, louder each time, until
the radiator seemed to be arguing with him.

    Miss Pruett taught fourth grade at Garfield School
and had a gentleman in Akron who wrote on blue paper
every Thursday. It was Saturday. I had sorted the mail
myself, and there had been no blue since the week of the
first frost. She sat with her back very straight and cut
her fried egg into small, exact squares, as if she were
going to grade them, and then she did not eat a single
one. "The yolks are lovely this morning, Mrs. Voss," she
said. They were. That was the trouble.

    Dewey Mott was the last of them, nineteen and all
wrists, back from the recruiting office in town. He had
gone down on Friday with his birth certificate folded in
an envelope as though it might be stolen. "They said my
ears," he told the sugar bowl. "Something in the left
one. I can hear fine." "You heard me call you down," I
said, and he laughed too quickly, and Mr. Halloran said
a man was better off out of it, and Miss Pruett passed
him the jam without being asked.

    I mention all this so it will be understood that I
notice things. A landlady who does not notice things is
only a woman who owns too many chairs. I poured the
coffee round and then I poured the last cup, at the far
end, at the place nobody sits. I lay that place every
morning, cup, saucer and spoon, for whoever comes down
late. My boarders know to leave it alone. It is a house
rule, like no hot plates and no callers after ten, and I
have never had to explain it.

    "Expecting company, Mrs. Voss?" Mr. Halloran said.
He said it kindly, which I did not care for. "Only the
usual," I said. Miss Pruett looked at the cup and then
at her plate of squares, and Dewey Mott looked at Miss
Pruett, and for a moment the three of them were very
interested in one another and not at all in me, which is
how I prefer it. I have nothing at my own table that
needs hiding. A landlady's business is everybody else's.

    When they had gone, Mr. Halloran to his casualties
and Miss Pruett to her Saturday errands and Dewey up the
stairs two at a time to lie on his bed, I sat down at
the far end. The coffee in the last cup had gone cold
and grown a skin. Raymond's letter was in my apron
pocket where it had been since Tuesday. Denver was very
busy, he wrote. Thanksgiving was out, but maybe the
spring. I read it again, though I knew it, and folded it
smaller than it had been. Then I poured the cup down the
sink and washed it and dried it and set it out again at
the far end, because a house does not run on maybe, and
breakfast is at seven.
```

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice; author and work are invented.

characters: Mrs. Voss, landlady and first-person narrator
Mr. Halloran, insurance salesman passed over for promotion
Miss Pruett, schoolteacher whose letters have stopped
Dewey Mott, nineteen, rejected by the recruiting office
Raymond, Mrs. Voss's absent son (only by letter)
blueprint.setting: A boarding house dining room on Tolley Street in a Lake Erie town, a Saturday breakfast in November, early 1950s
blueprint.situation: Mrs. Voss serves breakfast and catalogues each boarder's concealed disappointment, while keeping an extra place set; after they leave, the reader learns her son has written that he will not come for Thanksgiving.
blueprint.conflict: The narrator's pride in reading others versus her refusal to acknowledge her own grief; her boarders quietly see what she will not say.
blueprint.central_idea: Routine and attentiveness to others can serve as a shelter for one's own unadmitted disappointment.
blueprint.complexity: Mrs. Voss is perceptive and genuinely tender toward her boarders, yet her perceptiveness is also a defense; her claim of having nothing to hide is undercut by the extra cup and the letter. The ritual is both denial and stubborn hope, and the boarders' tact mirrors her own.

devices.quote: like a relative who has been told twice that there is no room
devices.function: Makes the radiator an unwanted petitioner, foreshadowing the absent son and the question of who has a place at the table.

devices.quote: until the radiator seemed to be arguing with him
as if she were going to grade them
devices.function: Shows Miss Pruett's control and orderliness masking her loss.

devices.quote: They were. That was the trouble.
devices.function: Implies that the morning's ordinary loveliness sharpens her disappointment.

devices.quote: only a woman who owns too many chairs
devices.function: Defines the narrator's identity through her noticing, revealing pride and loneliness.
The extra place stands for the absent son and her persistent hope.

devices.quote: I have nothing at my own table that needs hiding
devices.function: Her denial is contradicted by the cup and the letter.

devices.quote: I served at seven. I have always served at seven.
devices.function: Establishes routine as a defense, echoed in the final line.
Moves from wry public cataloguing to private grief.

devices.quote: Mr. Halloran did not tell me this. He told me
devices.function: Contrasts what boarders say and what they hide.

shifts.from: confident, wry survey of others' disappointments
shifts.to: private, restrained revelation of her own

blueprint.speaker: Mrs. Voss, a proud, observant landlady who narrates others' troubles precisely and her own only obliquely
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs; three portraits, a self-assertion, an exchange, and a solitary coda that recasts the extra place.

payload.premise: a boarding house breakfast where each guest hides a small disappointment

items.stem: Mrs. Voss's final action, in which she washes the cup and sets it out again (lines 62-63), primarily suggests that she

options.text: keeps her ritual of hope intact even after the letter has undercut it
options.why: She has read Raymond's refusal yet restores the place, holding routine and hope together.
options.label: correct

options.text: cares more for the house rules than for any person in her life
options.why: Overstates; the rules are a vehicle for her feeling for Raymond, not a replacement.
options.label: too_broad

options.text: has finally accepted that her son will never return to Tolley Street
options.why: Resetting the cup shows she has not given up; the letter even says 'maybe the spring.'
options.label: reversal

options.text: means to rebuke her boarders for asking about the empty place
options.why: The boarders have left; nothing suggests the act is aimed at them.
options.label: unsupported

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "keeps her ritual of hope intact even after the letter has undercut it". She has read Raymond's refusal yet restores the place, holding routine and hope together.
"cares more for the house rules than for any person in her life" is incorrect: Overstates; the rules are a vehicle for her feeling for Raymond, not a replacement.
"has finally accepted that her son will never return to Tolley Street" is incorrect: Resetting the cup shows she has not given up; the letter even says 'maybe the spring.'
"means to rebuke her boarders for asking about the empty place" is incorrect: The boarders have left; nothing suggests the act is aimed at them.

items.stem: The first-person point of view affects the reader's understanding of the passage chiefly by

options.text: allowing the narrator to confess her grief openly to the boarders over the course of breakfast
options.why: She answers 'Only the usual' and confesses nothing to them.
options.label: reversal

options.text: giving the reader equal access to the private thoughts of every boarder at the table
options.why: She infers from gestures and mail; she cannot enter their minds, as an omniscient narrator could.
options.label: wrong_function

options.text: suggesting that the narrator invents the boarders' disappointments out of plain boredom
options.why: Her inferences rest on evidence such as the mail she sorted; nothing hints at invention.
options.label: unsupported

options.text: detailing the boarders' troubles freely while withholding the narrator's own until the end
options.why: She explains each boarder's disappointment but mentions Raymond's letter only in the final paragraph.
options.label: correct

review_notes.key_flaw: The key calls both people 'concealing' their disappointments, but Dewey says his rejection openly ('They said my ears'). He is only partly in denial ('I can hear fine'). 'Similar disappointments' is fine; 'concealing' overstates it for Dewey.
